findings.title: removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete a federated recovery-codes credential
findings.body: When all recovery codes have been used, the authenticator calls authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId()). With this PR the credential may now live in an external user storage (obtained via getFederatedCredentialsStream in RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential), and removeStoredCredentialById only operates on locally stored credentials in the Keycloak DB. The removal silently does nothing for federated credentials, so the exhausted credential stays in the user storage and is never cleaned up (only the CONFIGURE_RECOVERY_AUTHN_CODES required action is added as a fallback). The delete path for federated credentials needs to go through the storage provider (e.g. disableCredentialType or an equivalent update) rather than the local stored-credential API.

findings.title: Federated recovery codes are never consumed, so they are infinitely reusable
findings.body: For local (Keycloak DB) recovery-code credentials, a successful authentication marks the used code as consumed (the recovery-codes credential provider updates the model on isValid). For credentials living in user storage, the validation path only calls the storage provider's isValid(); nothing notifies the storage that a code was used, and this reference storage implementation's isValid() for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel just checks membership in the stored list without removing the used code. The result is that recovery codes stored in user storage are single-use in name only and can be replayed indefinitely, defeating the purpose of recovery codes. There is no test asserting that a used code is rejected on a second login, so this regression is invisible in the test suite. Either the framework must drive consumption (e.g. via updateCredential on use) or the contract/test provider must implement and verify consumption.

findings.title: Raw (unhashed) recovery codes are passed to user storage via updateCredential
findings.body: createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generated codes to JSON and passes them as the UserCredentialModel value to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). For the local-storage branch, the credential provider stores only hashes of the codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues hashes them). A user storage that follows the pattern demonstrated by this PR's test provider will persist the plaintext codes (BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorage.updateCredential stores input.getChallengeResponse() directly as credentialData), which means recoverable plaintext secrets at rest in the external store and a weaker security posture than the equivalent local credential. At minimum the contract should be documented and the example/test provider should hash the codes on store; better, pass the pre-built credentialModel (with hashed secretData) instead of the raw codes.

findings.title: getCredentials NPEs when user is not present in the storage map
findings.body: The new getCredentials() implementation calls getMyUser(user) and immediately dereferences myUser.recoveryCodes without a null check. getMyUser can return null (users.get returns null), and every other method in this provider (isConfiguredFor, getDisableableCredentialTypesStream) guards against a null MyUser. Any Keycloak code path that calls getCredentials for a user not backed by this provider (or looked up by a mismatched username) will throw a NullPointerException instead of returning an empty stream.

findings.title: disableCredentialType does not handle recovery codes, leaving no way to remove the federated credential
findings.body: supportsCredentialType and updateCredential were extended to handle RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE, but disableCredentialType still only clears the OTP credential. Combined with the fact that removeStoredCredentialById does not work for federated credentials, there is no code path demonstrated that removes a recovery-codes credential from the user storage (admin REST disableCredentialType or account-console deletion will silently do nothing for this type). The test suite also never exercises removal/regeneration of federated recovery codes, so this gap is untested.

findings.title: Typo in authenticator config alias "delayed-suthenticator-config"
findings.body: The delayed-authenticator execution config is created with alias "delayed-suthenticator-config" (missing the 'a' in "authenticator"). This is copy-pasted from the existing pattern used in other tests; it works only because the delayed-authenticator provider apparently doesn't rely on the alias name, but it produces a confusingly named config object in the test realm and propagates the typo if copied further.
